explanations.answer: He investigates everything from the beginning
explanations.explanation: The writer says it seemed good to write after "…having carefully investigated everything from the beginning…" (Luke 1:3). The homework came before the pen. I respect that, baker. I once pulled a batch without checking the oven first, and the cookies told on me. Careful beats quick every time.

explanations.answer: He waits for a sign from heaven first
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a sign from heaven here. The writer says the writing came after having carefully investigated everything from the beginning (Luke 1:3). That's digging, not waiting. Waiting for a sign would be like me staring at a cold oven and hoping it warms up on its own.

explanations.answer: He copies the oldest account he finds
explanations.explanation: The writer says many had already undertaken to compose an account (Luke 1:1). But nothing says the writer copied one. The writer investigated everything from the beginning and then wrote an orderly account (Luke 1:3). Copying the oldest one would be like stamping a cookie with somebody else's name on it and calling it mine.

The writer says the goal is "…so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught." (Luke 1:4). That's the whole goal: Theophilus can know it for sure. No guessing and no fog. Just solid ground under his feet, like a good batch of dough that holds its shape.

The writer is going for the opposite of mystery. The goal is that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (Luke 1:4). Mystery is the key I shared a drawer with for years, the one that never figured out which door it opened. The writer wants Theophilus to know exactly where he stands.

The writer sets down an orderly account, and the reason given is certainty (Luke 1:3-4). I'm sure it reads beautifully, but beauty isn't the word in the verse. The aim is for Theophilus to be sure of what he has been taught. Pretty is nice, baker, but sure is the point.

The text says the opposite. Both Zechariah and Elizabeth were "…righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord." (Luke 1:6). That's how the text describes the two of them together. It doesn't describe a couple struggling to keep the commandments.

That's right, friend. Luke 1:6 says they were "…righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord." Both of them, together. I can't even keep a neat apron through one batch, so that kind of steady walking impresses me.
The text says Zechariah "…was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood…" (Luke 1:9). So this was the way the priests did it. Zechariah was chosen, and he went in to burn incense.
The text doesn't mention a high priest picking anybody here. It says Zechariah was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood (Luke 1:9). The lot did the choosing, friend.
The text never says Zechariah volunteered. It says he was chosen by lot (Luke 1:9). That was according to the custom of the priesthood, friend.

Yes, baker. Luke says that at the hour of the incense offering, "…the whole congregation was praying outside." (Luke 1:10). The whole congregation, not just a few folks. While Zechariah was inside, a crowd was outside praying.

The text says they were praying. At the hour of the incense offering, "…the whole congregation was praying outside." (Luke 1:10). The whole congregation, mind you. That's a lot of people praying outside.

explanations.answer: He is startled and gripped with fear
explanations.explanation: That's how Luke tells it: "…he was startled and gripped with fear." (Luke 1:12). Honestly, I'd be right there with him. If an angel showed up next to my oven, my mustache would be standing straight up. It's a very human reaction.

explanations.answer: He bows and asks the angel's name
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Zechariah bowed or asked a name here. It says he "…was startled and gripped with fear." when he saw the angel (Luke 1:12). The name comes later, when the angel offers it himself (Luke 1:19).

explanations.answer: He calmly finishes burning the incense
explanations.explanation: Calm isn't how the text describes him. It says he "…was startled and gripped with fear." (Luke 1:12). I think I'd have dropped the whole tray, and my hat would've gone with it.

Yes, baker. The angel says, "Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son…" (Luke 1:13). He says it right after telling Zechariah that his prayer has been heard. Think about it: this couple had no children (Luke 1:7), and this is the news that was coming.

The angel really does say it. His words are "Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John." (Luke 1:13). It comes right after he says the prayer has been heard. Good news, delivered by an angel, and it's right there in the verse.
The angel says more than that. He says "…many will rejoice at his birth…" (Luke 1:14). Many, friend, and he doesn't limit it to one household. This boy is going to be good news for a lot of people.

That's right. The angel says John will be a joy and delight to Zechariah, and then adds, "…many will rejoice at his birth…" (Luke 1:14). So the angel doesn't stop at Zechariah's joy. He says many will rejoice.
The angel says John "…will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb." (Luke 1:15). From his mother's womb, baker. That's before he's even born. I think that's a pretty big deal.

Solomon was Israel's king, and God gave him a wise and discerning heart (1 Kings 3:12). But that's not what the angel says about John. He says John will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb (Luke 1:15). Wise king, sure, but he's not who this verse is about.

Samson was a judge of Israel (Judges 16:31), known for his great strength (Judges 16:17). The angel doesn't say that about John, though. He says John will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb (Luke 1:15). No muscles mentioned, friend.

That's what the angel says. John will "…turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous…" (Luke 1:17). Two turnings in one sentence. The disobedient are the ones he turns to wisdom.

The angel doesn't name the Gentiles, meaning people who aren't Israelites, in this verse. He says John will turn "…the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous…" (Luke 1:17). Before that, he says John will turn many of the sons of Israel back to the Lord their God (Luke 1:16). So the verse is about the disobedient.

Rulers don't come up anywhere in the angel's words. He says John will turn "…the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous…" (Luke 1:17). I'll admit "rulers" sounds official enough to be right, like a cookie piled high with sprinkles. Looks impressive, but it's not what the recipe says.

The angel says John will "…make ready a people prepared for the Lord." (Luke 1:17). People, baker, not a building. It's about getting folks ready. That's close to my own job, helping bakers get ready for the big day.

Zechariah is standing in the temple right now, so it's an easy one to pick. But the angel says John will make ready "…a people prepared for the Lord." (Luke 1:17). The thing to get ready isn't a building. It's people.

The angel doesn't use the word kingdom here. He says John will "…make ready a people prepared for the Lord." (Luke 1:17). The preparing is for a people. Kingdom sounds grand, but it's not what the verse says.

explanations.answer: He and his wife are both old
explanations.explanation: Zechariah says, "I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years." (Luke 1:18). That's the reason he gives, and it matches what Luke told us earlier (Luke 1:7). I won't argue with a man about his age, friend. I don't even have one.

explanations.answer: He has never seen an angel before
explanations.explanation: Zechariah doesn't say that. He says, "I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years." (Luke 1:18). Seeing an angel did leave him startled and gripped with fear (Luke 1:12). But the reason he gives for his question is age.

explanations.answer: No priest has ever heard this before
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says that. Zechariah's reason is, "I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years." (Luke 1:18). He talks about himself and Elizabeth, and no other priest comes into it. Honestly, baker, the man isn't dragging the whole priesthood into this one.

explanations.answer: He will be silent and unable to speak
explanations.explanation: Gabriel says, "…you will be silent and unable to speak…" because Zechariah did not believe his words (Luke 1:20). When Zechariah comes out, he really can't speak to the people (Luke 1:22). The people realize he has seen a vision, and he keeps making signs to them (Luke 1:22).

explanations.answer: He will be blind until the boy is born
explanations.explanation: Gabriel doesn't say anything about blindness. He says Zechariah will be "…silent and unable to speak…" (Luke 1:20). When Zechariah comes out, he is unable to speak to the people (Luke 1:22). So it's his voice that goes quiet.

explanations.answer: He will lose his place as a priest
explanations.explanation: Gabriel says nothing about Zechariah's place as a priest. He says Zechariah will be "…silent and unable to speak…" (Luke 1:20). And Luke tells us that when his days of service were complete, he returned home (Luke 1:23). It's his voice that is affected.

explanations.answer: Until the day this comes to pass
explanations.explanation: Gabriel says Zechariah will be silent and unable to speak "…until the day this comes to pass…" (Luke 1:20). The silence lasts until the promise happens. That's a long stretch of quiet for a man with news to share. I can't go five minutes without talking, friend.

Gabriel doesn't tie it to the temple. And when Zechariah came out, he was still unable to speak (Luke 1:22). The silence is set for "…until the day this comes to pass…" (Luke 1:20). Walking out the door changed nothing.

explanations.answer: Until the end of his service
explanations.explanation: That's not what Gabriel says. The silence lasts "…until the day this comes to pass…" (Luke 1:20). His service ends, and he goes home (Luke 1:23). But Gabriel's timing is about the promise, not the end of his service.

Yes, baker. The text says that when Zechariah came out and couldn't speak, "…they realized he had seen a vision in the temple." (Luke 1:22). They'd been waiting for him and wondering why he took so long (Luke 1:21). He also kept making signs to them (Luke 1:22).

They do figure it out. Luke says, "…they realized he had seen a vision in the temple." (Luke 1:22). He still couldn't speak, and he kept making signs to them. Quite a puzzle for a crowd to solve, but they got there.

Elizabeth says, "In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people." (Luke 1:25). She gives the credit to the Lord. I think that's a lot to carry for a long time, and now it's lifted. A joyful moment, baker.

Elizabeth doesn't mention a fear of growing old. She says the Lord has "…taken away my disgrace among the people." (Luke 1:25). That's the thing she names. Luke did mention they were well along in years (Luke 1:7), but her words are about disgrace.

Elizabeth names something else. She says the Lord has shown her favor and "…taken away my disgrace among the people." (Luke 1:25). Grief over her family isn't in what she says. I think that's a lot lifted off her shoulders, friend.
